== Research Notes ==
=== Original Huntingdon will reviewed — 24 October 2026 ===

The original will names Taylor as John’s son, gives him a wagon and a joint share of the Antis home tract with James, and appoints James and Taylor executors. The existing Taylor Wilson account’s Antis household and reproduced 1889 obituary describing his removal with his father to a local farm in 1810 strongly identify this son. The obituary is a held transcription, not a newly inspected newspaper image. Conflicting inherited birth and death dates remain unchanged. The original will names wife Margaret, sons Richard, William, John, Samuel, Matthew, James and Taylor, and daughters Hannah and Jane. James and Taylor receive the 322-acre, 72-perch home tract jointly, subject to Margaret’s support and the legacies, and are appointed executors. The register records probate and the grant to both executors on 12 March 1825. The will names no mother for the children, no Hunter maiden surname, and no Scottish father for its testator. The widow Margaret is not automatically each child’s mother. The exact percentage assesses the complete father–child identification and is subjective. The original establishes the named family roles; identification of later adults, precise vital dates, maternal parentage and earlier Scottish ancestry require their own evidence. No live WikiTree save or vital-field change is made.<ref>[https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3QS7-L99B-T8NH?cc=1999196&wc=9PM6-7MN%3A268496101%2C268530601 Huntingdon County, Pennsylvania, Wills 1822–1847, volumes 3–4, register pp. 139–140; John Glasgow of Antis Township, will 21 January 1825, proved 12 March 1825; FamilySearch, Pennsylvania Probate Records, image 103 of 607. Original full page and both page details inspected 24 October 2026.]</ref>

Earlier dated statements below retain their source context; the original-will conclusions above supersede their uninspected-source and parentage assessments.

=== Individual father review, 22 October 2026 ===

This dated review supersedes any earlier grade of this pair within the stated record scope. The existing father [[Glasgow-1549]] is assessed at 64% (probable). Taylor Wilson’s exact 1 November 1798 birth and inherited family placement fit John’s c 1758 generation, allowing a paternal age around forty. The earlier William child is compatible with the same long family span.

Probable but dependent on the contributed family account; no held record explicitly names Taylor’s father.

Next useful test: Find the family-register or probate entry behind the exact birth date.

Source basis already held: [https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Glasgow-36 WikiTree profile export for Glasgow-36]. No new father attached; cited evidence and any inspected register entry are scoped above.

FULL OF YEARS.
Taylor W. Glasgow, a Nonogenarian [sic] of Antis Township Dead.

  Taylor W. Glasgow, of Antis township, died at his home near Bellwood,
Wednesday evening, March 27, in his 91st year.  Of Scotch-Irish
parentage he inherited those strong, hardy traits of mental and
physical character which mark the successful pioneer and made him in
many respects a remarkable man.  He was one of the few remaining human
links among us connecting the present century with the past, the
history of which, in its details of the manner, employment and
opportunities of life, reads to the generation of to-day like a
romance.  In 1821 he made a successful trip from Bellwood to Baltimore
in an ark laden with flour and whisky.  The voyage then was full of
perils.  Of the mementoes of that trip he was fond of exhibiting in the
latter years of his life a pocket-book and a vest which he had
purchased in the monumental city, and are doubtless well-preserved
relics among his effects to-day.
  He was born on All-Hallowe'en night, October 31, 1898, on the farm
where Mr. Joseph Hutchison now resides, a short distance east of this
city - long before Altoona or the Pennsylvania railroad were even a
possible conjecture in the brain of the enthusiast.  His recollections
and experience ran back close to the time when the red men of the
forest traversed this valley.  He removed with his father to the farm
now owned by Samuel Henderson in 1810, and, as indicating the physical
powers and endurance that marked his life, made a full hand in the
harvest field at the age of 13 years, and for seventy-five years had
never missed making a hand on that occasion.  He had never been sick
abed for a day, or had any use for medicines.  His last illness
confined him to his bed for less than a week, when he passed quietly
away as the flame dies out when the oil is exhausted.
  His religion was honesty and just dealing with his fellows.  He was
an exemplary citizen and held in high esteem by all his acquaintances.
In politics he was a democrat of the old school, voting for the
candidate of his party from the second term of Monroe to the second
candidacy of ex-President Cleveland.  In 1828 he married Miss Ann
Walker, to which union were given eight sons and daughters, six of whom
are living.  The sons are James P. and Frank M., living near the old
home, and Wilson, of Illinois.  The daughters are Mrs. William Rush,
and Mrs. W. G. Riley, of Bellwood, and Miss Angeline, at home.  Mr.
Glasgow's wife died December 7, 1887, in the 85th year of her age.

Altoona Tribune, April 4, 1889
